title: Older-adult social-platform fraud reports show a high-loss route that enforcement and redress do not yet close
source_unit: Federal Trade Commission Protecting Older Consumers 2025-2026 report and October 19, 2026 release
geography: United States; older-adult fraud reports submitted to the FTC Consumer Sentinel Network and selected FTC enforcement/redress matters

denominator.unit: Fraud reports submitted by older adults and selected enforcement/redress populations; report and case denominators are not a population estimate or one linked cohort

reported_older_adult_fraud_losses.value: about $600 million in 2020 to approximately $3 billion in 2025
reported_older_adult_fraud_losses.unit: reported losses in fraud reports from adults age 60 and over

reported_social_platform_investment_rout.value: investment-scam losses reported by older adults exceeded $1 billion in 2025, and the FTC says scammers often reached older adults through social media

age_loss_gradient.unit: U.S. dollars median reported individual loss among reporters age 80 and over in 2025

enforcement_redress_route.value: $3 million FloatMe redress order, more than $1.5 million refunded in September 2024, and more than $1 million in April 2026 payments to people who accepted their first payment; the settlement also required easier cancellation and a fair-lending program

recipient_recovery.value: not linked or measured for the older-adult fraud reports; individual delivery, acceptance, adequacy, account correction, repeat exposure, and durable trust remain open

observations.method: Structured extraction from the FTC annual report, its accompanying press release, and the report's cited enforcement/redress example. Reported losses, contact routes, age gradients, enforcement terms, and payment stages are retained as separate estimands.
observations.uncertainty: Consumer Sentinel data are selected reports, not a census of fraud, older adults, social-media exposure, or true loss. The report's older-adult fraud statistics and FloatMe redress example do not identify the same people, and reported loss does not establish platform causation, preventability, or household harm.
observations.subgroup: Adults age 60 and over who submitted fraud reports, with a highlighted age-80-and-over median-loss comparison; the FloatMe payment population is a separate case-defined group.
observations.counterinterpretation: The increase in reported losses may reflect reporting, scam composition, unusually large individual losses, platform use, or partner coverage as well as more fraud. Lower loss-report rates among older adults can coexist with higher median losses among those who do report.

related_sources.claim: The FTC report provides the 2025 older-adult fraud findings and selected enforcement examples.
The report PDF is the cited source for the annual-report findings and enforcement/redress discussion.

boundary: This record advances a bounded platform-exposure-to-remedy route for older adults: reported social-media contact and high-loss fraud are followed by enforcement and aggregate redress design. It does not establish true prevalence, platform causation, individual receipt or recovery, cancellation or fair-lending compliance in practice, restored household security, or durable trust.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Canonical FTC press-release URL string used as a stable source identifier; official report and PDF links are retained for reproduction.
